title: Egress access matrix and zone handoff proposal
summary: Workshop and proposal notes for a customer POC that needs controlled egress, split-DNS handoff across zones, and an access matrix for endpoints. Goal: provide a minimal-risk default architecture that satisfies regulatory constraints and offers staged complexity for rollout.
content:
Context:
This doc captures the design options we discussed in the POC workshop (2025-10-02) for a regulated-fintech customer who needs Redwood Private deployed into their VPCs. Requirements: locked-down egress, observable and auditable DNS handoff, cross-account/private connectivity to hosted runtime, and a pattern that supports multi-zone HA with deterministic failover.

High-level constraints and assumptions:
- Customer operates in AWS (primary), optional GCP for DR.
- No direct public internet egress allowed from model-serving subnets by default; all outbound must be controlled/approved.
- Traffic to Redwood hosted control plane allowed only via TLS to specific FQDNs; customers require IP allowlist alternative.
- Need to support S3/ECR access for model artifacts and optional telemetry shipping to SaaS observability endpoints.
- Must audit DNS resolution (who resolved what and to which IP).

Design goals (in priority):
1) Minimal blast radius: principle of least privilege for outbound flows.
2) Deterministic latency and failover between AZs and to Redwood endpoints.
3) Clear operational handoff: customers own network, Redwood provides prescriptive endpoint patterns and a small set of IP ranges/prefix lists.
4) Observability: per-route latency and per-token billing correlation retained.

Proposed architecture (phased):
Phase 0 — Locked sandbox (POC quick win):
- Single-customer VPC, two private subnets for inference nodes (AZ-a, AZ-b).
- No IGW in these subnets; egress via a dedicated egress VPC owned by customer (Transit VPC) using Transit Gateway (TGW) attachment.
- Egress VPC contains an outbound proxy (squid/nginx) in a public subnet with IGW. Proxy enforces allowlist, TLS interception disabled, TLS passthrough only.
- DNS: Customer Route 53 private hosted zone attached to VPCs. Conditional forwarder to an egress resolver in the egress VPC so that outbound resolution passes through an audited resolver (unbound + logs shipped).
- Connectivity to Redwood: outbound to Redwood hostnames over TLS; we provide a small set of static IPs via AWS Global Accelerator or customer-configurable NAT outside of serving subnets.
- Security groups: inference nodes allow egress only to proxy TGW attachment and to S3 endpoints.

Phase 1 — Production pattern with controlled endpoints:
- Replace public proxy with AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for communication to Redwood control plane where possible. Redwood publishes an Endpoint Service (interface endpoint) for management/control traffic.
- For data plane (inference traffic) we offer two models:
  a) PrivateLink streaming: Redwood deploys an Endpoint Service in our dedicated VPC and customer uses interface endpoints in their VPCs. This gives true private connectivity with SG-level control and no internet egress.
  b) Regional peered model: For high-throughput workloads where PrivateLink throughput may be limiting, use TGW peering to a Redwood-dedicated account and advertise routes via prefix lists.
- S3/ECR: Use gateway endpoints for S3 and interface endpoints for ECR and STS to avoid internet egress.
- DNS: Split-horizon R53 with conditional forwarding rules. Customer resolver forwards A/AAAA lookups for redwood-internal.* to Redwood’s DNS resolver IPs placed in a dedicated peering/VPC endpoint. We propose logging at the conditional forwarder and at the endpoint side for correlation.

Edge cases and operational considerations:
- Cross-account PrivateLink requires the customer to accept endpoint service; latency depends on AZ alignment. Recommend co-locating endpoints in each AZ used for serving.
- If the customer uses on-prem datacenter + AWS hybrid, use Transit Gateway Connect + NVA (e.g., wireguard/bgp) to carry traffic to egress VPCs and preserve DNS forwarding.
- Fallback behavior: if PrivateLink becomes unavailable, fallback to TLS over IGW via Global Accelerator IPs; define a strict failover policy in routing tables and TGW route priorities.
- Audit trail: every egress request must include a request id header injected by the proxy or local sidecar. We will surface this request id in Redwood access logs to correlate with token-level billing and traces.

Access matrix (example):
Columns: service | allowed path | required endpoint type | auth | audit mechanism
- Control plane API | PrivateLink / TLS to control-plane.redwood.ai | interface endpoint preferred | mTLS + API key | request-id + access logs
- Model artifact download (S3) | Gateway endpoint to aws:s3 + role-assumed signed URL | gateway endpoint | IAM role and signed URLs | S3 access logs + CloudTrail
- Telemetry ingest | TLS to telemetry.redwood.ai via PrivateLink or IGW | interface endpoint or IGW | mTLS | request-id + packet capture on proxy
- Model serving (data plane streaming) | PrivateLink (preferred) or TGW peering | interface endpoint / routed peering | mutual TLS | session logs + per-token metrics

DNS handoff pattern (detailed):
- Local VPC resolver (dhcp option sets) -> conditional forwarder for *.redwood-private to resolver in Redwood-managed peering VPC or to an interface endpoint IP.
- The resolver in the peering VPC is hardened (rate-limited, recursive off where unnecessary) and runs query logging to CloudWatch/ELK with username tags.
- For split-horizon entries (internal FQDNs that differ from public), Redwood provides a signed zonefile snippet and customers implement it in their private hosted zone as a CNAME or A record pointing to interface endpoint IPs. This keeps customer DNS authoritative while allowing us to change internal targets with minimal churn.

Security controls and guardrails:
- Prefix lists: Redwood publishes an official prefix-list for emergency allowlisting. Customers should prefer endpoint-based allowlist over IP allowlist.
- Security groups: default deny all; allow only SG-to-SG where SGs represent TGW endpoints and interface endpoints.
- IAM constraints: artifact pulls require cross-account role with limited trust and short-lived creds.

Observability and SLOs:
- Latency: instrument per-AZ p50/p95 p999 for PrivateLink and TGW paths.
- Availability: monitor endpoint health, route table fallbacks, and conditional-forwarder healthchecks. Define SLOs targeting 99.95% for control plane connectivity and 99.9% for heavy throughput data plane.
- Logs: DNS query logs, proxy egress logs, VPC Flow Logs aggregated per customer for 30 days (longer for enterprise).

Action items (next steps):
- [ ] Create minimal Terraform sample for Phase 0 (egress VPC + resolver) to share with customer — owner: Jonah (ETA 2025-10-15).
- [ ] Produce a PrivateLink onboarding checklist and acceptance flow for customer security teams — owner: Sofia (ETA 2025-10-17).
- [ ] Validate Global Accelerator static IPs vs customer egress policy with security — owner: Ravi (ETA 2025-10-14).
- [ ] Run a perf-run comparing PrivateLink vs TGW peering throughput for the customer's expected QPS — owner: Ava (ETA 2025-10-22).

Decision log (workshop outcomes):
- Decision 1 (2025-10-02): Use egress VPC + proxy for POC to avoid immediate changes to customer routing; agreed unanimously.
- Decision 2 (2025-10-02): Recommend PrivateLink as the long-term preferred pattern for control plane traffic; however, allow TGW peering for high-throughput data plane after perf validation.
- Decision 3 (2025-10-03): DNS split-horizon with conditional forwarding to a Redwood resolver is acceptable; customer wants query logs to be forwarded to their ELK within 24 hours.

Open questions for customer:
- Are there corporate proxy rules that disallow interface endpoints or PrivateLink? If yes, we need to adjust Phase 1 to TGW-only.
- Do they require on-premises network appliances for TLS inspection of artifacts? If so, TB discussion on signed URLs and artifact verification needed.

Notes and workshop artifacts:
- Attached whiteboard export: (see linked confluence CONFLUENCE-1234)
- Mini runbook snippet for failover and incident response included in the TF sample under the repo link above.

Appendix: simple ASCII diagram (Phase 1, preferred):

Customer-VPC-A (inference nodes) 
  | SG: inference-nodes-sg (egress only to endpoints)
  |--> Interface Endpoint (redwood-control) [ENI in subnet]
  |--> Interface Endpoint (redwood-data-az-a) [ENI in subnet]
  |--> Gateway Endpoint (s3)
  |
  +-> TGW attachment -> Transit/Egress VPC -> Private NAT/Accelerator (fallback to IGW)

Redwood-VPC (endpoint service)
  | endpoint service -> PrivateLink -> customer interface endpoint
